en: The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the All-Knowing Radiant Rishi’s Compassionate Mind and His Abstention from Eating Meat;
the translator's name is lost, now appended to the Qin Records.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha, at the site of the terrace of enlightenment, in the village of Migadāya, in the hermitage of the shrine of the Lord of the Gods (Īśvara).

At that time, there was a son of the Brahmin Kapila named Maitreya—his body golden in color, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, radiating silver light and adorned with gold like a mountain of white silver, his majestic brilliance immeasurable—who came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking in meditation within the grove together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

There were also five hundred matted-hair brahmins who, seeing from afar Maitreya’s dignified and composed deportment and his pure marks and signs, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, like a mountain of silver collapsing to form a heap of golden flowers interspersed with various jewels.
Golden flowers and golden pedestals, with fruits made of the seven treasures, were within the pavilions; from them issued sublime sounds that spoke in verse:
"I behold the Honored Muni, Whose countenance is ever pure and clear;
With the wondrous marks of a hundred blessings, He is peerless throughout the world."
The stains of affliction are forever exhausted, and wisdom is fully perfected;
with single-minded constancy I take refuge, body and mind free from weariness.
Therefore, with my five limbs prostrate, I desire to attain supreme peace and bliss.
"Liberated from suffering and free from fear, I pay homage to Śākyamuni.
At that time, when the various brahmins saw and heard this, they said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!..."
This youth possesses such dignified deportment and immeasurable radiance that he is no different from a Buddha;
under which Buddha did he first resolve his mind upon the Way?
"Whose sutras do you uphold?
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us!
The Buddha addressed the Brahmin Śikhaṇḍin:
"Listen attentively now!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you, so as to bring you joy!"

"In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a world named Supuṣpita, where the Buddha was named Maitreya; he constantly taught and transformed all beings through the four immeasurable states of mind characterized by loving-kindness."
That Buddha preached a sutra titled "The Great Ocean Cloud of Compassion and the Light of Maitrī Samādhi";
if there are those who hear it, they shall immediately transcend the sins of birth and death for hundreds of billions of kalpas and will certainly attain Buddhahood, without any doubt.
"At that time, there was in that country a great Brahmin named Sarvajñāprabha, who was wise and possessed of great knowledge, having extensively mastered numerous scriptures;
as for the worldly arts and crafts, there were none of the sixty-four skills in which he was not thoroughly practiced."

Hearing that a Buddha had appeared in the world and was preaching the *Maitrī-samādhi-prabhā-mahākaruṇā-sāgara-megha Sūtra*, he immediately challenged that Buddha with all the logical arguments and treatises of the world; yet, though he exhausted his eloquence and skill in debate, he could not defeat him.
Even though they have faith and submission as disciples of the Buddha and promptly resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they spoke these words:

"Now, within the Buddha-dharma, I shall recite and uphold the *Mahāmaitrī-samādhy-āloka-mahākaruṇā-sāgara-megha Sūtra*. By this merit, I vow that in the future, after incalculable eons, I shall certainly attain Buddhahood and be named Maitreya."
Thereupon, he left his home and entered the deep mountains, taking the growth of long hair as his outward mark and practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
For eight thousand years, he had few desires and remained free from worldly affairs; subsisting on alms-food, he recited and upheld this sutra, single-mindedly eliminating all distraction.
"At that time in the world, there appeared a shower of falling stars; the king was licentious and dissolute, comets streamed across the sky, and rain fell incessantly.
Floodwaters surged violently, and while the seer sat in meditative posture, he was unable to beg for alms for seven days."
At that time, in that forest, there were five hundred white rabbits, among whom was a rabbit king and his mate.
Seeing that the seer had not eaten for seven days, they spoke thus:
"Now this seer, for the sake of the Buddha-way, has not eaten for many days; his life is not far from its end."
"The banner of the Dharma is about to collapse; the ocean of the Dharma is about to run dry.
For the sake of the unsurpassed Great Dharma, I shall now ensure that it endures for a long time, even at the cost of my own body and life.
He then addressed the rabbits:
"All conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent; sentient beings cherish their bodies, yet they are born in vain and die in vain, never having acted for the sake of the Dharma.
I now wish to act as a great bridge for all sentient beings, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time, and to make offerings to the Dharma Master."
At that time, the hare king spoke these verses for the sake of the herd of hares:
"If there are any among the classes of animals Who hear the names of the Buddhas,
They shall forever leave the three evil realms And not be born in the eight states of no leisure."
If one hears the Dharma and practices it accordingly, one will always encounter the Buddhas in every place of birth;
with faith in the Dharma free from doubt, one takes refuge in the noble Sangha.
By following all the precepts and practices, one will thus swiftly attain Buddhahood.
"You shall surely attain Great Nirvāṇa, And forever experience unsurpassed bliss.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the hare-king addressed the hares, saying:
"I now wish to offer my body as an act of devotion to the Dharma; you all should each rejoice in accordance with this."

Why is this? Throughout many kalpas, I have lost my body countless times; driven by the three poisons, I took the forms of birds and beasts, living and dying in vain without ever acting for the sake of the Dharma.
Now, desiring to serve the unsurpassed Dharma, I wish to sacrifice my body and life to make offerings to the Dharma Master.
Then, the tree deity of the mountain immediately piled fragrant wood and set it ablaze; the hare king and his mother circumambulated the feet of the seer seven times and said:
"Great Master!..."
"I now wish to make an offering of the Dharma to the Venerable One.
The seer replied, "You are a beast;
though you possess a compassionate heart, by what means could you possibly provide such an offering?"
The hare said to the seer:
"I offer my own body as a gift to you, O Virtuous One, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time and all sentient beings may obtain great benefit."
Having spoken these words, he immediately said to his son:
"You may seek out water and grass as you please, but fix your mind in contemplation and maintain right mindfulness of the Triple Gem."
At that time, having heard what his mother said, the hare knelt and addressed her, saying:
"As Your Honor has spoken regarding the unsurpassed Great Dharma, if you wish to make an offering to it, I too am willing and joyful to do so."
Having spoken these words, he threw himself into the fire, and his mother followed him in.
At the moment the Bodhisattva sacrificed his body, heaven and earth shook violently; even as far as the Form Realm and all the devas, they rained down celestial flowers as an offering.
After the meat was cooked, the deity of the mountain tree addressed the seer, saying:
"The king of the hares, mother and son, have cast themselves into the fire for the sake of making this offering; now that the meat is cooked, you may eat it."

At that time, having heard the words of the tree deity, the seer was so overcome with grief that he could not speak. He placed the scriptures he had been reciting upon the leaves of the tree and further spoke this verse:
"Better to burn one's own body and destroy one's eyes than to bear to commit killing and eat living beings."

In the *Maitrī-sūtra* spoken by all Buddhas, it is said therein that one who practices loving-kindness would rather have their marrow broken and their skull exposed than bear to eat the flesh of sentient beings.
As the Buddha has taught, those who eat meat do not fulfill their practice of loving-kindness;
they constantly receive short lifespans and bodies plagued by many illnesses, sinking into the cycle of birth and death without attaining Buddhahood.
When that seer had spoken this verse, he made this vow:

"May I, in every lifetime, never give rise to the thought of killing, always refrain from eating meat, enter the White Radiance Samādhi of Compassion, and continue until the attainment of Buddhahood to establish the precept prohibiting the consumption of meat."
Having spoken these words, he threw himself into the fire pit to share his fate with the hare.
At that moment, the heavens and earth shook in six ways; by the power of the devas, the tree emitted a radiance, its golden brilliance shining forth and illuminating a thousand lands.

"At that time, the people of that country, seeing the golden light emanating from the mountain trees, followed the light until they arrived there. Having seen the rishi and the two dead rabbits lying within the fire, and having read the verses he had spoken as well as the Buddhist sūtra, they took these and returned them to the king."
When the king heard this Dharma, he proclaimed it to others and spread it abroad, so that all who heard it would give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śakra:
"You should know now that the White Rabbit King of that time was none other than I, the present Buddha Śākyamuni."
The hare at that time was none other than Rāhula;
the seer who recited the sūtras was none other than this son of a brahmin in the assembly, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya.

Fifty-six hundred million years after my parinirvāṇa, you shall attain the path of Buddhahood and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma at the site of the Vajrāsana beneath the Nāgapuṣpa Bodhi tree within the Flower Forest Garden, in the realm of the Cakravartin King Śakra.
The five hundred rabbits at that time were the present five hundred bhikṣus, including Mahākāśyapa;
the two hundred and fifty mountain tree spirits were the present two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, including Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana;
and the thousand kings were the present thousand bodhisattvas, including Bhadrapāla.
Those among the people of that king’s realm who hear this sutra are the disciples who receive the Dharma and attain the Way during the interval from my appearance in the world until that of Ruci.
The Buddha told Śakra:
“When Bodhisattvas seek the Dharma, they undergo diligent toil through kalpas, not sparing even their own bodies or lives;

though they may, as a result of karmic retribution, receive the body of an animal, they are always able to act for the sake of the Dharma, not sparing their own persons or lives, casting themselves into pits of fire to offer their bodies as an offering.”
They shall immediately transcend the sins of birth and death for nine hundred trillion kalpas.
Thereupon, they shall stand before immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and prior even to Maitreya, attain the Way of the Buddha.
"Why do you not diligently strive for the sake of the Dharma?
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the five hundred brahmins, Śreṇya and the others, sought ordination from the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome! At these words, his beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and his mind was suddenly enlightened; he attained arhatship.
Eighty thousand devas also resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had taught, each praised the conduct of the bodhisattvas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"After that seer had thrown himself into the fire pit, where was he reborn?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"At that time, having cast himself into the fire pit, that rishi was reborn in the Brahma world, where he universally expounded the Great Brahma Dharma for all beings. Eventually, he attained Buddhahood and turned the Great Brahma Wheel; the sūtras he preached were also titled 'The Light of Compassionate Samādhi and the Ocean-Cloud of Great Compassion.'"
Regarding the Prātimokṣa that has been established: one who does not practice loving-kindness is called a person who violates the prohibitions;

those who eat meat violate a grave prohibition and shall, in their future births, constantly drink molten copper, as described in the *Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Descent to Be Born Sūtra* when that seer attains Buddhahood.

Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and with hands clasped, knelt upright and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"The precepts taught by Maitreya when he attains Buddhahood prohibit the eating of meat out of a compassionate heart, regarding it as a grave transgression—how truly marvelous and extraordinary!
At that time, the great assembly, with one voice and in unison, all praised the precept against eating meat observed by the sentient beings of that land, saying:
"We vow to be reborn in that land!"
The World-Honored One prophesied that they would all attain rebirth there.
Venerable Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what name should this sutra be known?"
"How should this be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The essential core of this Dharma is titled 'The Bodhisattva White Rabbit King Sacrificing His Own Body and Life for the Unsurpassed Way,' and it is also titled 'The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the All-Knowing Radiant Seer’s Compassionate Heart and His Abstention from Eating Meat. You should receive and uphold it in this way."
The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for the Compassionate Heart of the All-Knowing Radiant Rishi Not Eating Meat.
